newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Dispute over parking in New York escalates at U.N.
newsitem.headline: Dispute over parking in New York escalates at U.N.

text.p: After a month of protests and statements over new New York parking rules for diplomats, a U.N. committee on Thursday has decided to buck the dispute up to the 185-nation General Assembly.
No date was immediately set for a meeting of the assembly, which could be called off if the United States meanwhile meets diplomats' objections.
The vote in the 15-member committee on relations with the host country -- which usually acts by consensus -- was 13 to 1, with the United States casting the only negative vote and Britain abstaining.

The United Nations legal counsel has ruled that parts of the programme, unveiled on March 10 and put into effect on April 1, violates international law on diplomatic immunity. Under the new rules, diplomats failing to clear their parking fines within 12 months would lose their special license plates.
Each country is also guaranteed two parking spaces outside its U.N. mission and one outside the residence of its ambassador, though this has not yet been fully implemented.
Many speakers said they would agree not to transfer the issue to the Assembly if the United States promised to defer the disputed provisions pending a satisfactory outcome.
The United States said the new measures would be applied flexibly while negotiations continued for a few more days, but this failed to satisfy most committee members.

The meeting was peppered with horror stories of envoys' vehicles being festooned with parking tickets even when properly parked, or seemingly targeted by vengeful police officers since the controversy hit the media.
One speaker complained that diplomats themselves were being turned into police by a new "hot line" for reporting unathorized vehicles parked in their reserved spaces.

Alexandre Zmeevski of Russia, who had taken a lead in pressing for General Assembly action, returned after taking a telephone call and said a Russian mission bus parked at a diplomatic space "is now being towed away by the New York City police," with its driver and passengers.
"Now, Mr. Chairman, there is a limit to everything. Every patience has its limits," he said.

He took the floor a few minutes later to ask for clarification of a report that Mayor Rudolph Giuliani had "allegedly, and I emphasise this, allegedly ... announced that the United Nations ... could get out of New York."

The mayor had just told reporters that "if they want to leave New York over parking tickets we can find another use for the neighbourhood. It happens to be some of the most valuable real estate in the world," Giuliani added.

A French diplomat who told a previous meeting it would "not be a tragedy" if the United Nations moved to another country, said more was at stake than parking. "That would be too trivial to be dealt with by the General Asembly. What we are talking about is diplomatic immunity and privileges."

A North Korean complained that a colleague parked at a diplomatic space found he had been ticketed 10 minutes later. When a member of the U.S. mission looked into the matter, they both found another ticket had been put on the car.
The representative of civil war-torn Zaire, Khabouji Lukabu, took issue with Giuliani for having said the United Nations should "pay more attention to Zaire than to parking."

"Let him be told that he should concern himself more with the safety of his own population," Lukabu said, referring to "all the incidents that take place daily in the subway, in the buses and the condition of the public transport systems that we are told to take in order to come to work. I myself would not take the risk."
